leading_positions.synthesis: All eight round-1 files name B012 as the preferred single-part prize, with the same two laureates (Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye). Shared: the magic-wavelength mechanism, accuracy and stability near 1e-18, reproduction in several laboratories and species, and use in tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. Not shared: the wording of the citation (some add magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms or the 10^-18 level, others do not), the weight placed on the pending redefinition of the second, and the stated fallbacks. Four members (Danielsson, Eriksson, Olsson, Pearce) state that they moved to B012 after reading the opening ballots, away from their own opening first choices or lower ranks (Danielsson had B039 first, Eriksson ranked B012 sixth, Olsson had B021 first, Pearce had B029 first). Several members add that they treat the support as a reason to scrutinise the candidate and not as merit in itself.

areas_of_agreement: The preferred configuration in all eight files is B012 with Katori and Ye, with no member proposing a different laureate set or a multi-part prize for the preferred configuration.

The scientific core is described consistently: the magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift, Lamb-Dicke confinement allows many neutral atoms to be interrogated on an ultranarrow transition, and fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reached and reproduced with Sr, Yb and Hg.

Several members describe the two-person credit as fitting under the three-laureate limit, in contrast to collaboration-scale candidates such as B039 and B029, where several members say the cap forces difficult exclusions.
No member reports a specific personal or institutional conflict with Katori, Ye or B012.
scientific_disputes: Seven members (all but Danielsson, who stresses the less dramatic discovery content) raise, as the strongest reservation, whether lattice clocks are a sufficiently distinct step beyond the frequency comb (2005) and single-ion control and ion clocks (2012), or an excellent refinement of an already honoured precision-timekeeping story.

Whether a precision-metrology capability is the right kind of result against a discovery about nature or a new class of quantum matter: Danielsson says B039 remains the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist, Johansson says B057 would be the better answer if the committee prefers a new quantum phenomenon, and Pearce notes the argument that IceCube or Higgs carry more weight with the wider community. Lindroth, Mehlig and Eriksson argue that the clock is both an invention and a discovery in the statutory sense.
Whether lattice clocks and ion clocks should be treated as one field needing joint recognition (Lindroth's question) or as a bounded invention.

The fallback options differ: B036 appears among alternatives for Danielsson, Eriksson, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson; B039 for Danielsson and Pearce; B010 for Kroll and Lindroth; B057 for Johansson and Mehlig; B051, B003, B005, B021 and B029 each appear once. No fallback is shared by more than five members, and these are alternatives, not preferred configurations.
attribution_disputes: Whether the two-name credit is complete: members cite NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other lattice-clock groups, Takamoto (Kroll) and ion-clock lines as contributors not credited in B012. Members describe the boundary as clean on paper but not verified from the supplied record.

Several members (Danielsson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce) say the early priority history of the magic-wavelength proposal and the relative roles of Katori and Ye rest on recollection or general knowledge and have not been independently verified. Katori is described as the concept and first realisation, Ye as the accuracy and stability frontier, but this division is not documented in the files.

For the fallbacks, members flag unresolved credit: B039 (four named people, Della Negra versus Virdee, leadership role versus scientific authorship), B057 (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang missing), B036 (earlier twisted-graphene theorists and Cao), B005 (Mathon and Umerski), B003 (Chu), and B029 (AMANDA and Baikal pioneers).
maturity_disputes: All eight members note that the formal redefinition of the second has not happened. Danielsson and Johansson treat this as a pending application. Eriksson, Kroll, Mehlig and Olsson describe waiting as a timing judgment, not a scientific doubt. Mehlig explicitly says it has no bearing on the science. Lindroth says part of the case rests on a pending application. Danielsson asks whether it is a precondition for recognition or a confirmation of impact.

Members differ on weighting prospective impacts (the redefinition of the second, clock-based geodesy, searches for varying constants) against demonstrated results. Olsson raises this explicitly; the others state which applications are already in use versus anticipated.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson discloses a specific connection to B051 (circuit and waveguide QED, Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, Chalmers colleagues Delsing and Wilson, co-author Kockum) and says recusal may be required there; she lists B051 only as an alternative and would not advocate it. She reports no conflict for B012.

Olsson would step back from deciding on B021, her opening first choice in transmission electron microscopy, if it were advanced, and notes that Johansson is also at Chalmers so any Chalmers-linked candidate needs a concrete check.
Eriksson flags field proximity, not a personal tie, for B005 and B036 and would defer to colleagues on recusal if either became the leading proposal.
Kroll notes a remote connection through time spent in John Hall's laboratory at Boulder, in the same precision-spectroscopy lineage as Ye, with no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye.

Lindroth flags field proximity to precision atomic physics for B012 without a specific conflict. Pearce notes closeness to the field of B029 and to the collaboration-credit issue in B039 from astroparticle and large-collaboration work, with no recorded tie to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS or any credited person. Danielsson and Mehlig report none.
questions_for_round2: Can the committee verify, from the supplied record and not from recollection, the priority and relative roles of Katori and Ye in the magic-wavelength proposal and early realisations, and is the two-name credit defensible against other lattice-clock groups?

Is the step from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes to lattice clocks a distinct contribution, and which citation wording best makes that boundary explicit: with or without magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and with or without the 10^-18 level?

Should the pending redefinition of the second be treated as a precondition, a confirmation, or irrelevant to the maturity of B012, and what is the committee's position on prospective versus demonstrated impact?

Does the committee regard a precision-metrology capability as the right kind of result for this year compared with a discovery about nature (B039, B029) or new quantum matter (B036, B057), and what would have to be true about attribution in these alternatives to make any of them competitive with B012?

Do any disclosed flags (Johansson on B051, Olsson on B021, Eriksson on B005 and B036, Kroll's remote Hall connection) need a formal ruling on recusal or on how a member's statements are weighed if the alternatives are advanced?
summary.chair_observation: All eight members converge on one preferred configuration, B012 with Katori and Ye, and four of them (Danielsson, Eriksson, Olsson, Pearce) state that they moved to it after reading the opening ballots. This is convergence in round 1 and not evidence of merit, as several members say themselves. The remaining differences are about the novelty margin over the 2005 and 2012 prizes, the unverified priority history, whether other lattice-clock groups are omitted, and the timing relative to the redefinition of the second. Alternatives are scattered and none is shared by a majority. The chair has counted only positions explicit in the eight files.
